title: Family of man fatally shot by Montreal police officer to sue following acquittal
article: The family of a Black man fatally injured by a Montreal police SWAT team member in March 2016 will be suing the City of Montreal, the Montreal police force and the officer in question following his recent acquittal.

On Thursday, a Quebec Court judge acquitted officer Christian Gilbert, 51, of manslaughter, ruling that he did not use excessive force when he shot a rubber bullet at Bony Jean-Pierre, 46, who had been attempting to escape from a drug raid at a Montreal North apartment.
"(We) firmly believe that his death was preventable had the officer Gilbert acted in a sensible and reasonable manner," the daughters and wife of the man said in a statement.

Jean-Pierre was trying to flee through the first-storey window of an apartment on Arthur-Chevrier St. when Gilbert shot him in the head, causing injuries that led to his death in a hospital four days later. Gilbert testified that he'd been aiming for the man's hip to knock him back into the apartment after firing a warning shot that had been ignored - a testimony Judge Yvan Poulin said he believed on Thursday.

The family said it is devastated by the court's decision, calling Gilbert's use of force excessive and Jean-Pierre's death preventable. The sum of damages it plans to sue for has not yet been determined, but lawyer Michael N. Bergman, who is representing the family, suspects it will be "reasonably significant."
"(We) had hoped to see Officer Gilbert held accountable for his negligent and unreasonable actions, which led to the reckless death of Bony Jean-Pierre," the family said.
Both the family and Bergman take issue not with where the man was hit, but with the fact that he was shot to begin with.

"The judgment seems to have been focused quite narrowly on the physics ... of whether or not the plastic bullet could have hit the deceased in the hip or in the head, and ignores the problem that the deceased was no threat to anybody," Bergman said.
The decision sets a precedent for the extent to which people in positions of authority, like police officers, can use force when it isn't necessary, he added.

"This wasn't somebody running down the street and they were trying to stop him by, for example, shooting him in the legs, this is somebody in a confined area, trying to get out of a window," Bergman said. "There was no reason to shoot him with a plastic bullet or any other device, any other projectile, anywhere, because he could've just been apprehended and stopped."

The raid during which Jean-Pierre was shot was part of an investigation by the Montreal police, who had purchased drugs in the building while undercover a few days earlier. In a briefing leading up to the raid, police were informed the people in the apartment could be armed. Jean-Pierre was among several other men when police showed up.
The man's family says the police version of the ensuing events differs from those by witnesses, and it thinks the system has let down yet another person of colour.

"(We) unfortunately believe that Bony Jean-Pierre has become another statistic, with the result that the senseless deaths of people of colour will continue to occur at the hands of the police without any consequence," they said.

After the judge's decision was delivered on Thursday, Gilbert's lawyer, Louis Belleau, was reminded by reporters that Jean-Pierre's death touched off a fierce protest by people who believed the victim had been racially profiled.

"(The) decision in no way says that we should lower our guard or be less vigilant towards the problems of discrimination or racial profiling or discrimination towards minorities, in particular Black people. We have to be constantly vigilant," Belleau said. "But in this case there is no dimension that can lead one to think that there was an ingredient that was racial that influenced the conduct of the police. It was an operation on a group of criminals who were distributing drugs in an apartment."

Jean-Pierre, in particular, had a criminal record that included convictions for assault, unauthorized possession of a firearm and uttering threats. In 1993, he was sentenced to a six-year prison term for armed robbery.
Bergman said that while it is his duty to respect the judgment of the court, things should have played out differently.
"Apparently, the building itself was more or less surrounded," Bergman said of the raid. "So, why fire on this individual when there is no real or an apparent danger from this man?"
"(Thursday's) decision itself does not refer to race," Bergman added, "but you cannot help but speculate and wonder ... what would have been the situation had the deceased been white?"
